papers.title: Black adults show cross-sectional associations between sleep quality and episodic memory retention: an investigation of underlying factors.
papers.abstract: Non-Hispanic Black adults have poorer sleep quality than non-Hispanic White adults (hereafter, Black, White), which may underlie disparities in cognition. Epidemiological evidence suggests episodic memory may be more sensitive to poor sleep quality in older Black adults as compared to older White adults. Related exacerbating factors of these differences, such as depression and discrimination, are understudied. Here, we aimed to determine mediators of associations between sleep quality and episodic memory retention in an adult lifespan sample (18-74 years) of Black and White adults. We measured sleep quality, depression, and discrimination using self-report questionnaires, and assessed memory retention using a context memory task. We assessed if sleep-memory associations were moderated by age and mediated by depressive symptoms. We also assessed if discrimination mediated the association sleep-memory associations, controlling for age and years of education. In Black and White adults, higher depressive symptoms were associated with poorer sleep quality. Black adults demonstrated reliable sleep-memory associations and associations among higher discrimination, higher depressive symptoms, poorer sleep, and poorer memory, but we found no significant mediation effects. Depression level might affect sleep quality regardless of race or age. Black adults may demonstrate poor memory retention because of associations among discrimination, depression, and sleep.

papers.title: Aloysia deserticola (rica-rica) essential oil impairs inhibitory synaptic transmission in hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons.
papers.abstract: Aloysia deserticola is an aromatic plant native to the Chilean Andean highlands that has traditionally been used in herbal preparations. Although a previous behavioral study reported the anxiolytic and antidepressant-like effects of rica-rica essential oil in an animal model, its neurophysiological actions at cellular and synaptic levels remain largely unexplored. In this study, we characterized A. deserticola essential oil (AD-EO) using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and examined its acute effects on GABAergic synaptic transmission via whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from CA1 pyramidal neurons in acute dorsal hippocampal slices obtained from C57BL/6 J mice. GC-MS analysis revealed an enriched thujone chemical profile, with peaks tentatively identified as α- and β-thujone accounting for 89.06% and 3.38% of the total chromatographic area, respectively. Application of AD-EO to the bath reduced evoked inhibitory postsynaptic current (eIPSC) amplitude in a concentration-dependent manner and shortened eIPSC decay kinetics. This is consistent with a postsynaptic contribution to the suppression of inhibitory signaling. At intermediate-to-high estimated thujone-equivalent concentrations, AD-EO increased the paired-pulse ratio. Coefficient-of-variation analysis supported the presence of an additional presynaptic component. Consistent with these findings, AD-EO reduced the frequency and amplitude of miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents. Furthermore, the effects on eIPSC amplitude and the paired-pulse ratio were reversible following washout. Together, these results demonstrate that AD-EO suppresses inhibitory synapses in CA1 pyramidal neurons via effects consistent with pre- and postsynaptic locus. These results provide electrophysiological evidence that AD-EO modulates hippocampal inhibitory transmission and support further investigation of the mechanisms underlying the neurophysiological actions of this complex natural preparation.

papers.title: Resistance training volume for major depressive disorder: the MoveMind randomized controlled trial protocol.
papers.abstract: This randomized controlled trial aims to investigate the effects of resistance training (RT) volume (high vs. low) and non-exercise group on depressive symptoms, remission rates, adherence and the psychological and neurobiological mechanisms underlying these effects in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD). A total of 150 adults (18-59 years) diagnosed with MDD will be randomized into three groups: high-volume RT (HV, n=50; 4 sets of 10-12 repetition maximum [RM]), low-volume RT (LV, n=50; 2 sets of 10-12 RM), and a non-exercise control group (CG, n=50). Participants in the intervention groups will train three non-consecutive days per week for 8 weeks. The primary outcome, depressive symptoms, will be assessed by a psychiatrist using the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale. Secondary outcomes will include potential psychological mechanisms (perceived self-efficacy, affective responses to exercise, and well-being), assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and at the 3-month follow-up, and neurobiological mechanisms assessed by inflammatory and metabolic biomarkers related to MDD pathophysiology, including TNF-α, IL-6, IL-10, IL-1β, CRP, IGF-1, BDNF, insulin, glucose, and cortisol, measured before and after the intervention. Tertiary outcomes will include dietary intake and ultra-processed food consumption (24-hour dietary recall), body composition (DXA), muscular strength, and sleep quality. Intervention efficacy will be analyzed using intention-to-treat linear mixed-effects models. The findings may contribute to more effective, personalized, and sustainable RT prescriptions that improve adherence and complement conventional treatments for MDD. https://ensaiosclinicos.gov.br/rg/, identifier RBR-9tn4ncp.

papers.title: Style transfer mapping with ensemble learning for cross-subject EEG-based neuropsychiatric disease recognition.
papers.abstract: Cross-subject electroencephalogram (EEG) recognition remains a fundamental challenge because large inter-subject variability causes severe distribution shifts that substantially degrade the generalization ability of existing learning models. Most existing transfer learning methods attempt to align global feature distributions but often overlook subject-specific structural variations, resulting in unstable adaptation under limited calibration data. To address this problem, we propose a Prototype-Consistent Style Transfer Mapping (PC-STM) framework for cross-subject neuropsychiatric disease recognition. Unlike conventional domain adaptation methods, the proposed framework models subject discrepancy as a prototype-guided style transformation that explicitly aligns target representations with class-consistent source prototypes while preserving discriminative structures. Specifically, a multi-source prototype construction strategy is introduced to characterize representative class distributions, followed by a confidence-aware transductive semi-supervised style transfer module that iteratively refines transformation parameters using labeled calibration samples and unlabeled evaluation samples. Furthermore, a reliability-aware ensemble learning strategy dynamically aggregates multiple subject-specific classifiers according to their calibration consistency, thereby improving robustness against heterogeneous subject distributions. Experiments on two public EEG datasets covering major depressive disorder and Parkinson's disease show stable performance under the evaluated leave-one-pair-out protocol. The calibration labels are inherited from the public dataset cohorts or task conditions, and the study does not constitute prospective clinical diagnostic validation. Beyond the evaluated EEG tasks, prototype-guided style transfer may provide a basis for future investigation of other limited-supervision recognition problems.

papers.title: Effect of mindfulness breathing versus acupoint stimulation on anxiety, fatigue, and sleep quality among children undergoing stem cell transplantation: a three-arm randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Children undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) commonly experience anxiety, fatigue, and sleep disturbances, which may negatively affect their quality of life and recovery. Non-pharmacological interventions, including mindfulness breathing and acupoint stimulation, have emerged as supportive approaches for symptom management. This study evaluated and compared the effects of mindfulness breathing, acupoint stimulation, and routine care on anxiety, fatigue, and sleep quality among children undergoing HSCT. A three-arm randomized controlled trial was conducted at the stem cell transplantation unit of Tanta University Hospitals, Egypt. Ninety children aged 7-17 years were randomly assigned to three equal groups: control (routine care), mindfulness breathing, and acupoint stimulation. The assigned interventions were delivered once daily for seven consecutive days before transplantation and continued for one month after transplantation. Anxiety, fatigue, and sleep disturbance were assessed using the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory for Children, Fatigue Severity Scale, and PROMIS Parent Proxy Sleep Disturbance Scale, respectively. Assessments were conducted at baseline, one week, and one month after intervention. Baseline sociodemographic and clinical characteristics were comparable among the three groups. Significant Group×Time interactions were observed for diastolic blood pressure, respiratory rate, pulse rate, anxiety, fatigue severity, and sleep disturbance scores (p < 0.001). Both mindfulness breathing and acupoint stimulation resulted in significant improvements compared with routine care. Mindfulness breathing demonstrated greater improvements across several physiological and psychological outcomes compared with acupoint stimulation and routine care. Mindfulness breathing and acupoint stimulation are promising complementary interventions for improving physiological and psychological outcomes among children undergoing HSCT. Mindfulness breathing showed greater improvements across several outcomes and may represent a useful supportive nursing intervention during the transplantation period. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are recommended to confirm the sustained effects of these interventions. The Pan African Clinical Trial Registry PACTR 202407894821147. Date: 17 July 2024. www.http://pactr.samrc.ac.za.

papers.title: Interval-based cycling for wheelchair users with spinal muscular atrophy: feasibility, tolerability, and exercise effects.
papers.abstract: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) often leads to wheelchair use and sedentary lifestyle. Previous exercise studies suggest that prolonged exercise may cause fatigue and limit feasibility. We assessed feasibility and tolerability of interval-based assisted cycling in wheelchair users with SMA and explored potential effects on symptoms, motor performance, and metabolic outcomes. In this exploratory self-controlled crossover study, 15 wheelchair users with SMA completed three test days separated by a control period and an 8-week home-based exercise intervention. Assessments included questionnaires on pain, constipation, fatigue, sleep quality, and quality of life, along with lung function, blood sampling, and cycle testing. Training consisted of 10 min of assisted interval cycling five times weekly. No clinically meaningful changes were observed in primary or secondary outcomes. Nevertheless, attendance was high (95%), no exercise-related dropouts occurred, and no systematic increase in fatigue was observed. During exercise testing, participants increased their heart rate by an average of 42 bpm, indicating cardiovascular engagement. Interval-based assisted cycling was feasible and well tolerated in wheelchair users with SMA without inducing excessive fatigue. Although no clinically meaningful group-level effects were observed, interval training enabled cardiovascular engagement despite severe motor impairments.

papers.title: The clock-output gene DBP regulates muscle insulin sensitivity and its fluctuations.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythm disruption is associated with metabolic disorders, yet the role of clock genes in glucose metabolism remains unclear. D-box binding protein (DBP) is a clock output gene that activates the D-box, and we used systemic Dbp knockout (KO) mice to investigate DBP's role in glucose metabolism. We generated two independent KO mouse lines. Intraperitoneal insulin tolerance tests (IPITTs) were performed in 13-week-old male mice at zeitgeber time (ZT) 1 and ZT 13. To assess hepatic and muscle insulin sensitivity, we examined 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2DG) content and AKT phosphorylation followed by transcriptome analysis using muscle. In the KO mice, enhanced insulin sensitivity was observed in ZT1 following IPITT compared to wild-type (WT) mice, but not in ZT13. These findings indicate that while systemic insulin sensitivity fluctuates throughout the day in WT mice, it does not fluctuate in KO mice. Increased glucose uptake and AKT phosphorylation in gastrocnemius muscle (GM), but not the liver, were observed in KO mice at ZT1. Plasma nonesterified fatty acid (NEFA) levels were reduced during the inactive phase in KO mice. Muscle transcriptome analysis identified chemokine and cytokine-related pathways as the most enriched, including C-C motif chemokine ligand 5 (CCL5) and its receptor C-C chemokine receptor type 5 (CCR5). Muscle insulin sensitivity oscillates, with a reduction during the inactive phase. This study demonstrates that DBP deficiency suppresses circadian fluctuations of muscle insulin sensitivity, likely via plasma NEFA and CCL5-CCR5 signaling. DBP plays a role in circadian regulation of muscle insulin sensitivity.

papers.title: Subtle Alterations of Tidal Breathing Variables in Healthy Late Preterm Neonates at Term-Equivalent Age.
papers.abstract: Late-preterm birth is associated with increased respiratory morbidity, but tidal breathing at term-equivalent age remains incompletely characterized. We hypothesized that healthy late-preterm neonates would differ from term neonates, with the between-group difference in tPTEF/tE designated as the primary outcome. In this prospective cross-sectional study, 60 healthy late-preterm and 60 term neonates underwent tidal breathing analysis (MasterScreen PAED) at term-equivalent age (40 weeks' postmenstrual age) during natural quiet sleep without sedation. Late-preterm neonates had lower tPTEF/tE (27.4 ± 7.0% vs. 31.2 ± 6.9%; Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted p = 0.028; Cohen's d = 0.544) and VPTEF/VE [28.6 (25.1-31.0)% vs. 32.1 (27.3-35.5)%; adjusted p = 0.028; Cliff's δ = 0.304] than term neonates. Respiratory rate was higher (53.2 ± 9.1 vs. 49.6 ± 9.5 breaths/min), but not significant after correction (adjusted p = 0.126). No other tidal breathing variables differed significantly after correction. In the primary multivariable model, each additional week of exact gestational age was associated with a 1.18-percentage-point increase in tPTEF/tE after adjustment for sex, body weight, and crown-heel length (B = 1.182; 95% CI, 0.540-1.823; β = 0.323; p < 0.001). When postnatal age replaced gestational age, the association was inverse (B = -0.167/day; 95% CI, -0.263 to -0.071; β = -0.306; p < 0.001). At term-equivalent age, healthy late-preterm neonates had modestly lower tPTFEF/tE and VPTEF/VE than term neonates. These findings may reflect subtle maturational differences in expiratory flow dynamics associated with late-preterm birth.

papers.title: Prospective Associations of Diet Quality During Pregnancy With Cardiovascular Health (Life's Essential 8) Among Women in Midlife.
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular health (CVH) often declines in midlife. Diet during pregnancy, a similarly sensitive period involving physiological changes, may influence long-term CVH, but few studies have examined this relationship. We examined the associations between diet during pregnancy and CVH in midlife. Participants are 776 women enroled in Project Viva during early pregnancy (1999-2002, mean 32.7 years). Participants completed food frequency questionnaires during the first and second trimesters, from which we calculated three diet scores (higher scores = better diet): Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH), Mediterranean Diet (MD) and Dietary Inflammatory Index (DII × -1). We averaged scores across trimesters and generated internal z-scores. At the midlife visit (2017-2021, mean 51.1 y), we assessed CVH using the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 (range 0-100; higher scores = better CVH), including behavioural (diet, physical activity, sleep, smoking) and biomedical (BMI, blood pressure, lipids, glucose) subscores. We assessed associations using linear regression adjusted for age, race and ethnicity, nativity, education, parity, marital status and income at enrolment. Most participants were non-Hispanic White (70%) and college graduates (76%). Mean midlife CVH score was 76.3 points. Higher (per 1-SD) DASH z-scores were associated with better overall (β 3.3; 95% CI 2.2-4.3), behavioural (3.5; 2.5-4.4) and biomedical (3.1; 1.5-4.7) CVH scores. Higher MD z-scores were associated with better overall CVH (2.4; 1.4-3.4), behavioural (2.6; 1.6-3.5) and biomedical (2.6; 1.0-4.2) scores. Higher DII (× -1) z-scores were associated with better overall CVH (2.6; 1.6-3.7), behavioural (2.7; 1.7-3.7) and biomedical (2.5; 0.9-4.1) scores. A better pregnancy diet was associated with higher CVH scores for diet, physical activity and BMI, and both DASH and DII with blood pressure. Women who consumed healthier diets during pregnancy had better CVH two decades later. Dietary assessment in pregnancy may identify women at risk for both short-term and long-term health problems.
papers.journal: Journal of human nutrition and dietetics : the official journal of the British Dietetic Association

papers.title: The Impact of 12-Hour Versus 8-Hour Shifts on Intensive Care Unit Nurses' Physical and Mental Well-Being and Job Satisfaction: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Twelve-hour shifts have been widely implemented in intensive care units (ICUs), where nurses work in high-acuity environments requiring sustained clinical attention. However, evidence regarding the impact of shift length on ICU nurses' physical health, mental well-being, job satisfaction and patient-care outcomes remains limited and inconsistent. To investigate the impact of 12-h compared with 8-h shifts on ICU nurses' physical health, well-being and job satisfaction. This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines and was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251021178). A systematic search of CINAHL, Ovid MEDLINE and Embase was conducted in February 2025 and updated in June 2026. Additional searches of Scopus and Web of Science were undertaken in June 2026. Eligible studies included ICU nurses and compared 12-h with 8-h shifts. Risk of bias and methodological quality were assessed using design-specific Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal tools and the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach. Findings were synthesised narratively due to the heterogeneity of the included studies. Of 815 records identified, five studies met the inclusion criteria. Findings on fatigue, sleep and burnout were inconclusive across studies. Twelve-hour shifts were generally associated with greater roster satisfaction, flexibility and work-life balance, while evidence for sick leave was limited or mixed. Evidence did not consistently favour either 12- or 8-h shifts for ICU nurses, with low to very low certainty of evidence. Shift duration should therefore be considered alongside overall roster design, staffing needs and nurses' well-being when planning ICU schedules. Nurse managers should avoid a one-size-fits-all approach to shift duration, as evidence does not clearly favour 12- or 8-h shifts. Shift-length decisions should consider roster design, staffing needs, workload, recovery time and nurses' preferences. Managers should also monitor staff well-being, satisfaction, absenteeism, retention and patient-care outcomes when reviewing shift patterns. Given the low certainty of evidence, ongoing local evaluation is essential to ensure rosters support workforce sustainability and safe, high-quality care.

papers.title: Seizures, Sleep, and the Midnight Sun.
papers.abstract: The well-known bidirectional link between seizures and sleep may be most conspicuous in environments where the chief zeitgeber - sunlight - undergoes extreme but consistent changes over the course of a year. Routine circannual encounters with the midnight sun and midday darkness strategically position Earth's polar regions as natural laboratories to study this effect. We reviewed 2337 studies that related status epilepticus (SE), light exposure, and sleep in people in the Arctic or Antarctic. Status epilepticus represented the most extreme - and arguably incontrovertible - expression of seizure. After applying filters and exclusion criteria, 5 studies were included for SE and 36 for sleep. Status epilepticus was correlated with increasing daylength going into summer (ie, brighter sunlight vector) at high latitudes. Sunlight and chronotype demonstrated a linear relationship, with more sunlight going into summer (ie, brighter sunlight vector) advancing chronotype, less sunlight going into winter (ie, darker sunlight vector) delaying chronotype, and extreme cases becoming free-running in either vector direction. U-shaped relationships were also surmised, with increased sleep fragmentation and decreased sleep duration for both brighter and darker sunlight vectors. A parsimonious synthesis is that a brighter sunlight vector advances chronotype to shorten and fragment sleep, thereby triggering more SE and seizures. Although these data are derived from Earth's poles, they are not specific to polar regions; rather, they hold ramifications for everyone on planet Earth - 1 in 10 of whom will have a seizure in their lifetime.

papers.title: EEG-based brain effective and functional connectivity predict PET-defined amyloid positivity in cognitively normal individuals.
papers.abstract: Early identification of amyloid-beta (Aβ) pathology is essential for timely intervention in Alzheimer's disease (AD), as Aβ accumulation precedes clinical symptoms by years. We predicted positron emission tomography (PET) -defined Aβ status in cognitively normal individuals using non-invasive resting-state dry electroencephalography (EEG). Brain effective and functional connectivity were quantified to characterize dynamic information transfer between regions. Features derived from dynamic brain connectivity were used to train machine learning models for Aβ classification. EEG-based models can predict amyloid positivity with accuracy comparable to, or in some cases exceeding, that of plasma p-tau217 and previously reported predictors based on cognitive measures, demographics, and health factors, depending on the model. Beyond near real-time Aβ inference, the framework identifies the most affected brain regions and connections associated with neurodegeneration, offering complementary information to blood-based biomarkers and supporting its potential as an affordable tool for early AD detection in primary care and population screening.
papers.journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

papers.title: Sleep Strategies and Performance Outcomes in Ultramarathon Runners: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Ultramarathon events impose prolonged physiological and cognitive demands, often spanning 1 or more nights with limited sleep opportunity. To examine associations between pre-race and intra-race sleep strategies and physical and cognitive performance outcomes in ultramarathon runners. PubMed, EMBASE, PsycINFO, SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to July 25, 2025. Primary observational or experimental studies published in English, or available in English translation were eligible when they involved ultramarathon runners (>42.2 km) and reported sleep as a variable of interest in relation to race performance or cognitive performance. Systematic review. Level 3. Two reviewers independently extracted study design, participant characteristics, race characteristics, sleep outcomes, performance outcomes, and cognitive outcomes. Methodological quality was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklists. Nine studies involving 2262 participants were included, with overall low risk of bias. Of the 4 studies examining pre-race sleep, 3 reported a significant association or group difference with a race-performance outcome. Reduced sleep was generally associated with poorer physical and cognitive performance. Greater intra-race sleep duration was consistently associated with longer finish times, reflecting additional nonmoving time and increased sleep need in longer events. Greater pre-race sleep duration, including sleep extension, was associated with faster finish times, and better pre-race sleep quality was linked to higher cognitive performance. Pre-race sleep extension was associated with faster finish times, although the observational evidence does not establish causality. Further research using objective sleep measures and controlled designs is required.

papers.title: Optical, Morphology, and Structural Characterization of Synthesized Eco-Friendly Silver Nanoparticles for Potential Antibacterial Applications.
papers.abstract: In this work, the silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) were synthesized by an eco-friendly biosynthesis using Bougainvillea spectabilis leaf extract, which acts as reducing and capping agent. The AgNPs were analyzed using UV spectroscopy, FTIR spectroscopy, XRD, and scanning electron SEM. From the UV-visible spectral analysis we recorded an SPR peak at 415 nm, which is characteristic of spherical AgNPs. The results obtained from FTIR suggest the potential role of biomolecules in reducing Ag+ and the capping of AgNPs. The XRD pattern demonstrated the FCC crystalline of metallic silver, showing average crystallite size ranging from 30 to 50 nm. Results obtained from the SEM revealed the morphology and size distribution of synthesized AgNPs. From the images obtained, we determined a spherical morphology with an estimated size distribution measuring 50-200 nm. Furthermore, the AgNPs exhibited strong antibacterial behavior against tested bacterial strains, namely Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. These results highlight that the silver NPs are sustainable for potential biomedical and environmental applications.

papers.title: Intimate Partner Violence Around the Time of Pregnancy and Infant Safe Sleep Practices.
papers.abstract: Does intimate partner violence (IPV) before or during pregnancy increase the likelihood of unsafe infant sleep practices (surface sharing and non-supine positioning) among women with a recent live birth? The sample included 213,556 women with a recent live birth participating in the 2016 to 2022 Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS) from 41 U.S. jurisdictions. We analyzed PRAMS data to estimate the prevalence of physical IPV 12 months before or during pregnancy and infant sleep practices (i.e., surface sharing and supine positioning) by demographic characteristics. We calculated adjusted odds ratios (aORs) to examine associations between physical IPV and infant sleep practices. Overall, 3.2% (95% confidence interval [CI] [3.1, 3.3]) of women reported physical IPV in the 12 months before or during pregnancy. Experiences of physical IPV in the 12 months before or during pregnancy were significantly associated with an increased likelihood of reporting surface sharing in the 2 weeks before survey administration and those who had experienced physical IPV had 20% higher odds of putting their infant in a non-supine sleep position compared to those who had not experienced IPV (aOR = 1.2, 95% CI [1.1, 1.4]). Physical IPV before or during pregnancy may be an important risk factor for unsafe infant sleep practices. Attention to IPV as a potential barrier to safe infant sleep practices may be an important consideration for perinatal care and support.

papers.title: Making sense of touch: Spatial tactile cues promote efficient visuo-somatosensory integration and restore motor accuracy under sensory conflict.
papers.abstract: Effective interaction with complex environments relies on the integration of somatosensory and visual signals into coherent spatial representations of the body in external space. When these signals conflict, as during goal-directed hand movements under mirror-reversed visual feedback, motor performance deteriorates. Despite this conflict, the visual mapping between the hand and the environment remains preserved, and visual information typically facilitates motor performance, whereas tactile feedback impairs it. Here, we tested whether providing tactile input with explicit spatial structure renders visuo-somatosensory integration functionally relevant and stabilizes motor behaviour under sensory conflict. Healthy adults performed a mirror-tracing task, tracing a shape's contour with the index finger while tactile feedback conveyed either motion-related cues alone or additional discrete spatial landmarks aligned with the outline. Spatially structured tactile cues preserved movement accuracy and smoothness relative to motion-related tactile input, indicating more effective online motor control. EEG source analyses further revealed that, when spatial tactile cues were present, somatosensory activity increased and functional connectivity was largely restricted to sensorimotor areas. In contrast, when tactile cues did not convey spatial information, sensory conflict was associated with widespread reductions in cortical activity, including in somatosensory and parietal areas, and with a diffuse functional connectivity pattern consistent with elevated sensorimotor uncertainty. Together, these findings indicate that providing spatial structure to tactile input can mitigate the detrimental effects of visuo-somatosensory conflict on motor performance and support more efficient integration of visual and somatosensory information during action. KEY POINTS: Accurate movements depend on combining visual and somatosensory information to estimate the position of the body in external space. When these signals conflict, motor performance usually deteriorates and tactile feedback can become disruptive. We tested whether tactile feedback becomes useful for movement control when it provides explicit spatial landmarks, rather than only motion-related information from finger-surface contact. During a tracing task under visuo-somatosensory conflict, spatially structured tactile cues preserved movement accuracy and smoothness compared with when touch conveyed motion cues alone. Spatial tactile cues were associated with increased somatosensory cortical activity and a more spatially restricted pattern of functional coupling within sensorimotor networks, whereas their absence was associated with reduced somatosensory and parietal activity and a more distributed connectivity profile. Spatial structure in touch promotes multisensory integration, helping stabilize motor control under sensory conflict and highlighting how tactile cue design may improve sensorimotor function.

papers.title: Sequential Associations of Sleep Architecture, Nocturnal Oxygenation, and Respiratory Disturbance With a Composite PSG-Derived Rhythm-Event Index.
papers.abstract: Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB), particularly obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), has been associated with cardiovascular complications including cardiac arrhythmias. However, the relative contributions of respiratory, oxygenation, and sleep architecture indices to composite PSG-derived rhythm-event index remain incompletely understood. To investigate the sequential associations of sleep architecture, nocturnal oxygenation, and respiratory disturbance indices with the composite PSG-derived rhythm-event index in patients undergoing polysomnography (PSG). Demographic, respiratory, oxygenation and sleep-architecture variables were extracted from PSG records. The primary outcome was a composite PSG-derived rhythm-event count, estimated as round(arrhythmia index × TST_hours) from the PSG-exported arrhythmia index, which was calculated during total sleep time only. Negative binomial regression used an offset of log(TST_hours). Because the outcome demonstrated overdispersion, negative binomial regression with an offset of log(TST hours) was used. Because the original 14-predictor model was over-parameterized for the sample size, a six-predictor model (age, sex, BMI, AHI, T90, and sleep efficiency) was chosen post hoc. This reduced model was not prespecified before the original analysis. Sleep efficiency was retained because it showed a strong signal in the exploratory 14-predictor model. The resulting p-values should therefore be interpreted as optimistic and exploratory. A sequential model-building approach (Model 1: age, sex, BMI, AHI; Model 2: plus T90; Model 3: plus sleep efficiency) was used to document the incremental contribution of each domain. A fully adjusted 14-predictor model was fitted only as a supplementary analysis. Wald 95% CIs and bootstrap percentile 95% CIs (2000 resamples) are reported. Forty-one participants were included (mean age 47.8 ± 13.5 years; median BMI 29.4 kg/m2). Severe OSA (AHI ≥ 30 events/hour) was present in 56.1%. Median arrhythmia index was 3.2 events/hour, with marked overdispersion. In the six-predictor model, only higher sleep efficiency was associated with lower arrhythmia rate (IRR = 0.946 per 1 percentage-point increase, 95% CI 0.921-0.972, p < 0.001; bootstrap 95% CI 0.888-0.984). T90 was associated in the Wald inference (IRR = 1.034, 95% CI 1.006-1.063, p = 0.016) but this association was not robust under bootstrap resampling (95% CI 0.979-1.067). AHI was not associated with arrhythmia rate (IRR = 1.000, 95% CI 0.987-1.014, p = 0.954). Age, sex and BMI were also not significant. A 14-predictor exploratory model had a marginally lower AIC (411.4) but a substantially higher BIC (438.8), consistent with overfitting. In this exploratory selected sleep-center cohort, AHI and other respiratory-event indices were not independently associated with the composite PSG-derived rhythm-event index. Only higher sleep efficiency showed a robust association with lower arrhythmia rate, but this finding is hypothesis-generating and may reflect unmeasured confounding. These results require confirmation in larger prospective studies and should not guide clinical risk stratification.

papers.title: Incidence of Intensive Care Unit Delirium After Heart Surgery: A Feasibility Study of a Forest Environment Intervention.
papers.abstract: Postoperative delirium is a serious complication in intensive care units (ICUs), particularly following cardiac surgery. It is associated with circadian rhythm disruption, sleep disturbances and adverse outcomes. ICU environments often lack natural time cues, which may exacerbate circadian misalignment and increase delirium risk. The primary aim of the study was the evaluation of the implementation of two chronotherapeutic ICU interventions regarding recruitment, implementability and safety. Its secondary aim was to descriptively assess postoperative delirium across intervention groups. This randomized feasibility study was conducted in a tertiary cardiac surgery ICU in Austria. Adult patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery were allocated to one of three groups: (1) forest environment, (2) light exposure or (3) standard ICU care. Interventions were applied for 12 h daily. Delirium was assessed at three postoperative time points using the confusion assessment method for the ICU (CAM-ICU) and intensive care delirium screening checklist (ICDSC). This study was conducted between March 2020 and 2025. Seventy-seven patients were enrolled, and 64 remained in the final analytical cohort. Interventions were delivered within routine care. Patients and ICU staff did not report intervention-related concerns. Implementation challenges included ICU restructuring, patient transfers due to COVID-19 and deviations from randomized allocation because of operational constraints. No intervention-related adverse events occurred. Delirium assessments were limited at several time points because of sedation, early ICU discharge or transfer. Across all groups, postoperative delirium was detected in 5 of 130 CAM-ICU completed assessments (3.8%) and 8 of 115 ICDSC completed assessments (6.9%), precluding inferential group comparisons. Chronotherapeutic environmental interventions were feasible and safe in ICU care. Feasibility results highlighted challenges related to ICU logistics, sedation-related assessment limitations and pandemic-related disruptions. The unexpectedly low delirium incidence limited conclusions regarding intervention efficacy. Future trials should include larger high-risk populations and prospectively defined feasibility outcomes. Optimized ICU environments, including noise reduction and light management, may support delirium prevention. Chronotherapeutic environmental interventions are feasible additions to routine ICU care.

papers.title: Recurrent convexity subarachnoid hemorrhage mimicking transient ischemic attack in cerebral amyloid angiopathy: A case report.
papers.abstract: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is an important cause of spontaneous convexity subarachnoid hemorrhage in elderly patients and may present with transient focal neurological episodes that closely mimic transient ischemic attack. We report a 73-year-old man who presented with recurrent, stereotyped episodes of dysarthria and abnormal sensation in the left hand, initially suspected to represent transient ischemic attack. The symptoms developed during sleep, were presumed to have occurred almost simultaneously, lasted approximately 10 to 15 minutes, and resolved completely. Brain magnetic resonance imaging performed on the day of symptom onset revealed acute convexity subarachnoid hemorrhage in the right cerebral convexity, with cortical superficial siderosis and cerebral microbleeds on susceptibility-weighted imaging. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed no acute ischemic lesion, and magnetic resonance angiography revealed no responsible vascular abnormality. The patient fulfilled the Boston criteria version 2.0 for probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy. His symptoms were attributed to transient cortical dysfunction related to acute convexity subarachnoid hemorrhage rather than cerebral ischemia. Antithrombotic therapy was not initiated because of the hemorrhagic risk associated with cerebral amyloid angiopathy and the absence of a high-risk embolic source. Levetiracetam was administered during hospitalization because focal seizure could not be excluded, but it was discontinued after discharge. During more than 1 year of follow-up, he remained stable without recurrent neurological symptoms or hemorrhagic events. This case highlights the importance of recognizing cerebral amyloid angiopathy-related convexity subarachnoid hemorrhage as a transient ischemic attack mimic.
papers.journal: Journal of cerebrovascular and endovascular neurosurgery

papers.title: Radiomic Signatures From Conventional MRI Predict Recovery in Obstetric Brachial Plexus Palsy: A Machine Learning Approach in Infants.
papers.abstract: Obstetric brachial plexus palsy (OBPP) causes variable neurological outcomes, but early prognostic biomarkers remain limited. This study evaluated whether radiomic features extracted from routine T2-STIR MRI can predict functional recovery in infants with OBPP, and whether combining these features with routinely available clinical predictors improves prognostic performance. In this prospective single-center study, 39 infants with OBPP (mean age 12.5 ± 5.7 weeks) underwent 3 T MRI during physiological sleep. Postganglionic lesions were semi-automatically segmented on coronal T2-STIR images, and 111 radiomic features were extracted per patient. After a minimum two-year clinical follow-up (mean 25.5 ± 2.0 months; range 24-32 months), patients were classified as having complete (n = 17) or partial recovery (n = 22). Feature selection was performed using the Boruta algorithm. Five supervised machine learning models were trained and internally optimized on the training set (n = 28) using leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV), and their performance was subsequently evaluated on an independent holdout test set (n = 11). A clinical model (Narakas classification, birth weight, pseudomeningocele) and a combined clinical-radiomic model, summarized as a nomogram, were additionally developed. Eight radiomic features, including shape, first-order, and texture metrics, differentiated recovery groups. Among the radiomics-only models, SVM-RBF performed best (training AUC = 0.929, F1-score = 0.889; test AUC = 0.867, F1-score = 0.750), followed by random forest (training AUC = 0.952; test AUC = 0.783); test-set specificity was low for several classifiers. The combined clinical-radiomic model outperformed the radiomics-only model (training AUC = 1.000; test AUC = 0.933, accuracy = 0.818), and the bias-corrected calibration curve of the nomogram showed good agreement with observed outcomes (mean absolute error = 0.07). Radiomic analysis of routine T2-STIR MRI shows promise for predicting recovery in OBPP, and its combination with simple clinical predictors further improves discrimination. Given the small sample size and the performance drop between training and test sets, these findings should be regarded as preliminary and hypothesis-generating, and require validation in larger, multicenter cohorts before clinical use.

papers.title: Circadian regulation of antiviral susceptibility and treatment efficacy: A translational gap.
Insertable Cardiac Monitoring in Pediatric Patients: A Real-World Single-Center Experience With a New-Generation Device.
papers.abstract: Insertable cardiac monitors (ICMs) are increasingly used in pediatric patients, yet data on new-generation devices remain limited. The aim of this retrospective study was to describe a single-center real-world experience with a new-generation ICM in pediatric patients, focusing on procedural feasibility, sensing performance, transmission burden, and user experience. Consecutive patients aged ≤18 years undergoing LUX-Dx ICM implantation between 2023 and 2025 were included. Procedural characteristics, sensing parameters, transmission patterns, diagnostic yield, reprogramming strategies, and patient/caregiver-reported experience were analyzed. Data are reported as median (25th-75th percentile) or mean ± standard deviation. Twenty-nine patients underwent ICM implantation. Procedures were brief (6 ± 2 min) and complication-free. Electrical parameters were satisfactory and stable at discharge. Follow-up was 18 (6-23) months. A median of 2.7 transmissions per patient-month were received, of which 55% were alerts. Time from arrhythmia detection to transmission was 15 (3-21) hours. The number of episodes per patient was 4.8 (3.1-15.9) per month, with substantial inter-patient variability and bradycardia being the most frequent detection (80%). A diagnostic conclusion was reached in 79% of patients (positive: 45%, negative: 34%) at a median of 3 months. Reprogramming was performed in 90% of patients, mainly remotely (77%), and was predominantly directed toward reducing detection sensitivity. Patient and caregiver acceptance of remote monitoring was high. In pediatric patients, new-generation ICM implantation was safe, well tolerated, and associated with stable sensing performance. Remote monitoring and reprogramming enabled timely diagnosis and individualized optimization, supporting the clinical utility of contemporary ICMs in this population.

papers.title: Breathing-evoked potentials in humans during wakefulness and sleep.
papers.abstract: Breathing modulates cortical activities and cognitive functions, but the neurophysiological basis of the brain-breathing relationship is incompletely understood. We aimed to determine whether breathing at rest evokes scalp EEG-detectable potentials (as inspiratory occlusions do in the respiratory-related evoked potential model), whether these signatures persist during sleep and whether they are linked to sleep-organizing processes. We examined recordings from 729 participants in the Cleveland Family Study to identify cortical activity time-locked to inspiration during wakefulness and sleep, with a median of 7871 respiratory cycles analysed per participant. Breathing-related cortical responses were assessed in the time and frequency domains. Quiet breathing evoked a reproducible sequence of cortical potentials during wakefulness, including a pre-inspiratory component ∼300 ms before inspiration and several post-inspiratory peaks ≤3 s after. These responses persisted during non-rapid eye movement stages 2 and 3 (N2 and N3) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, in which they showed simplified morphology resembling K-complexes and co-occurred with increased spindle-range activity. The pattern was present irrespective of body mass index and was qualitatively unchanged in the 203 participants free of sleep-disordered breathing, arguing against obesity or sleep apnoea as its origin. Scalp EEG can detect breathing-evoked potentials during quiet breathing in awake humans. These potentials persist during sleep with a morphology that resembles cortical activities previously associated with sleep stabilization. Further studies are needed to determine the physiological and clinical significance of these observations in health and disease. KEY POINTS: Spontaneous breathing at rest evokes reproducible breathing-related cortical potentials detectable with scalp EEG. These potentials persist during sleep. They are associated with time-locked modulation of cortical oscillatory activity.

papers.title: Prenatal lifestyle associations with maternal and infant metabolic biomarkers: secondary analysis of the PEARS RCT.
papers.abstract: Maternal lifestyle factors may influence maternal and newborn metabolic biomarkers. Composite healthy lifestyle scores (HLS) have been developed but remain understudied among maternal high-risk populations, such as pregnant women with overweight or obesity and their offspring. Therefore the aim of this study was to investigate associations between a Healthy Lifestyle Score (HLS) and its components in early and late pregnancy with metabolic biomarkers among women with overweight and obesity and their newborns. Secondary analyses were conducted with data from the PEARS trial. HLSs were created based on self-reported lifestyle habits (diet, physical activity, alcohol, smoking, and sleep) for 334 and 285 women in early and late pregnancy, respectively. Linear regression analyses examined associations of HLSs and its components with maternal biomarkers (fasting glucose, insulin, c-peptide, cholesterol, triglycerides, complement component C3, C-reactive protein, leptin, adiponectin, interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumour necrosis factor alpha) in early and late pregnancy and in cord blood. Benjamini-and-Hochberg corrections were applied to account for multiple testing. Across all analytical models, a higher HLS and non-smoking status in early pregnancy were significantly associated with higher maternal HDL cholesterol and lower IL-6 levels, respectively. Most of the other associations, primarily those involving smoking and physical activity levels and maternal or infant inflammatory biomarkers, were robust across models but not all withstood correction for multiple testing. Having an overall healthy prenatal lifestyle, particularly not smoking and being physically active in pregnancy, show some benefits for lipid and inflammatory biomarkers.
papers.journal: Nutrition, metabolism, and cardiovascular diseases : NMCD

papers.title: Association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden in NCAA Division I athletes.
papers.abstract: To examine the association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden among NCAA Division I athletes and whether sleep difficulty is associated with neurocognitive performance. This cross-sectional analysis included 584 NCAA Division I student-athletes. Sleep difficulty was assessed using the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire Sleep Difficulty Score (SDS), and symptom burden using the 24-item SCOAT6 Symptom Evaluation. Symptom number was analyzed with multivariable negative binomial regression and symptom severity with multivariable linear regression using HC3 robust standard errors. Models adjusted for age, sex, sport type, and head-injury history. Sensitivity analyses excluded overlapping sleep-related symptoms and examined individual symptoms, symptom domains, head-injury strata, and neurocognitive outcomes. Each 1-point increase in SDS was associated with greater symptom number (n = 583; IRR = 1.127, 95% CI 1.086-1.169, P < .001) and severity (n = 584; B = 1.054, 95% CI 0.688-1.419, P < .001). Associations persisted after excluding sleep disturbance and after additionally excluding fatigue/low energy and drowsiness. Twenty-one of 24 symptoms remained associated with SDS after false-discovery-rate correction. Head-injury history did not modify associations with symptom number (P = .971) or severity (P = .846). SDS was not associated with memory (B = -0.012, P = .269), executive function (B = -0.017, P = .247), or psychomotor speed (B = 0.001, P = .939). Greater self-reported sleep difficulty was associated with greater baseline concussion-like symptom burden but not with assessed neurocognitive outcomes. Sleep difficulty should be considered a contextual factor when interpreting baseline concussion symptom reports.

papers.title: Multidimensional sleep health and risks of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: A MAIHDA-based prospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: The combined and interactive effects of multiple sleep dimensions on mortality remain unclear. We applied Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy (MAIHDA) to examine how multidimensional sleep health relates to all-cause and cardiovascular mortality. The analytic sample included 4340 adults for all‑cause mortality and 3790 for cardiovascular mortality from the Sleep Heart Health Study. Six sleep dimensions were dichotomized into healthy versus unhealthy categories and combined to form 64 unique strata representing all possible sleep health profiles. Individuals were nested within strata in multilevel Cox MAIHDA models. Three models were estimated: model 1 (null), model 2 (sleep-domain fixed effects), and model 3 (sleep-domain fixed effects plus covariates). In null models, sleep‑health strata explained 8.51% of the variance in all‑cause mortality and 15.01% in cardiovascular mortality, indicating meaningful heterogeneity across sleep profiles. After accounting for sleep-domain main effects and covariates, most between‑strata variance was explained (PCV = 99.95% for all-cause mortality and 78.32% for cardiovascular mortality), indicating that mortality risk was predominantly additive rather than driven by unique non‑additive combinations. Healthier continuity and timing were associated with lower all-cause mortality, while timing was the most consistent sleep feature for cardiovascular mortality; absence of sleep disorders showed a weaker association mainly for all-cause mortality. Strata with multiple unhealthy sleep dimensions consistently had the highest marginal standardized predicted 10-year mortality risks. MAIHDA maps mortality risk across multidimensional sleep profiles and quantifies additive versus non-additive effects. Mortality risk was explained primarily by the additive accumulation of sleep-health attributes.

papers.title: From consensus to evidence: Bridging the gap in pharmacotherapy for insomnia and sleep dysfunction in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: This letter commends the Parkinson Study Group for their comprehensive consensus on sleep in Parkinson's disease while addressing critical gaps in insomnia and depression management. It emphasizes the need for evidence-based pharmacotherapies, avoiding off-label sedating antidepressants, and prioritizing rigorously designed clinical trials for non-motor sleep disturbances.
